full_judgment:
4. Sub-Inspector of Gulshan Police Station started investigation of the case but later on handed it over to Mr Md Zahidul Islam, Sub-Inspector, RAB-1, Uttara, Dhaka as Home Ministry (Law Section-2) vide Memo No. (স্বাঃ মঃ (আইনঃ২) র‌্যাব ১/২০০৭/৯৩৯ dated 19-10-2007 and Reference No.৩/৪৭----০৭/২৪৫৭ dated 28-10-2007 entrusted him with the investigation who submitted police report under Table 5 and 9 Kha of section 19(1) of the Narcotics Control Act, 1990. According to him, Ice Pill was recovered which according to Chemical Examination Report contains Amphitamin and Diethyl and Toluene, chemicals which found place in the Kha category of Schedule of Table-1 of section 19(1) of Narcotics Control Act, 1990. 

 5. The case was transferred to Druta Bichar Tribunal No. 4 for trial. The petitioner raised the question before the Tribunal that, since investigation has not been held under the provision of Narcotics Control Act, 1990, then the proceeding is illegal. The said application having been rejected, the petitioner moved this court and obtained these Rules. 

 6. The accused petitioner on medical ground obtained bail on 15-5-2008. The bail obtained on medical ground was stayed by the State before the Appellate Division in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 39 of 2008 till disposal of Criminal Miscellaneous Case by this court. The accused petitioner thereafter, moved before this court again on 30-7-2008 for bail on medical ground and a Division Bench of this court again enlarged the accused petitioner on bail purely for treatment outside of the custody. Again this order was stayed by the Appellate Division. 

 7. Mr Anisul Haque, learned Advocate, appearing for the accused-petitioner, submits that, since on the earlier occasion (3-6-2008) the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court stayed the order granting bail to the accused petitioners till disposal of the Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 4678 of 2008 and Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 4679 of 2008 by this court, now the learned Advocate prayed for disposal of the Rules on merit and further submits, that question fallen in these two Rules being purely relating to interpretation of law, it can be heard and disposed of without there being any counter-affidavit filed by the State. 

 9. The question being purely raised on a law point i.e. whether officer of RAB-1 could investigate a case of Narcotics Control Act, 1990. 

 10. Section 39 of the Act where power for investigation has been given in the case fallen in the categories of the Act. Let us quote section 39 of the Act, Section 39 of the Act is Power of Investigation of Director General, etc: 

 11. On a pure reading of this section, it appears that, offence of a case is to be investigated by the Director General of the Narcotics Department who can exercise the power of an officer-in-charge of a police station for investigation of an offence under this Act. Government also has power to investigate the offence under this Act, by any officer subordinate to the Director General. Now the question which calls for determination is that under sub-section 2 of section 39 of the Act, whether Government for investigation of a case can appoint anyone who was not an officer of the Narcotics Control Department. Sub-section 2 provides that Government can investigate any offence in this Act, by an officer who is sub-ordinate to the Director General of Narcotics Control Department, not by a person who is not in the Narcotic Control Department. Subordinate to Director General means an officer who is subordinate to the Director General of the Narcotics Control Department. It is true, Government by notification in the official Gazette, appointed an inspector of RAB-1, Uttara, Dhaka but RAB-1 is not under the control of Narcotics Control Department and in no way it can be said that the inspector is an official subordinate to the Director General. It is to be borne in mind that Narcotics Control Act, 1990 is a special law where power to investigate in a case provided under section 44 and power of search, etc provided under section 36 and some other powers have also been given under the Act. An officer of RAB is not answerable to the Director General, as such, not subordinate for the authority of the Director General to investigate an offence. Special Law is not ordinary Law. Criminal Procedure Code differentiates offences in two categories, offences under Penal Code under section 28 and offences under other laws under section 29. In the decisions of State vs Sakur Ali, 9 BLC 238 and Masud Rana Babu vs State 12 BLC 196 it has been held that under special law the provisions of general or civil law does not apply unless special law makes room for the same. 

 12. Now, the question is, whether an Inspector of RAB is subordinate to Director General of Narcotics Department or not. As per Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary, International Student's Edition 'Subordinate' means having less power or authority than else in a group or an organisations a person who has a position with less authority and power than else in an organisation. In the decision of RG Jamb vs Republic of India, AIR 1963 SC 550 it has been held that 'By the use of the word 'sub-ordinate' without any qualifying words, the Legislature has expressed its legislative intention of making punishable such subordinates also who have no connection with the functions with which the business or transaction is concerned. An Assistant Controller of Imports in the office of the Joint Chief Controller of Imports and Exports is subordinate of the Joint Chief Controller though the acceptance of the bribe has nothing to do with the appeal pending before the Joint Chief Controller, thus subordinate means and stands as inferior in rank, grade, class or order dependent upon the authority or power of another i.e. subordination in rank not subordination of function. It appears that the investigation was started illegally by a sub-inspector of Gulshan Police Station and thereafter, Government further committed illegality by transfer of the case to RAB-1 who has done the investigation but without provision of the Act. Law does not provide for investigation of an offence fallen under this Act by an outsider other than an officer of the Narcotics Department. The investigation done by an officer of RAB-1 is without any sanction of law. In similar situation, in the case of Balabir Singh vs State, 3 Supreme Court Cases 299 it has been held as : 

 "Under section 41(1) only an empowered Magistrate can issue warrant for the arrest or for the search in respect of offences punishable under Chapter IV of the Act, etc when he has reason to believe that such offences have been committed or took place. Likewise, only empowered officers or duly authorised officers as enumerated in section 41(2) and 42(1) can act under the provisions of the BDPS Act. Under section 41(2) only empowered officer can give the authorisation to his sub-ordinate officer to carry out the arrest of a person or search as mentioned therein. The Legislature intended that certain Magistrates and certain officers of higher rank and empowered can act to effect the arrest or search. This is a safeguard provided having regard to the deterrent sentences contemplated and with the view that innocent persons are not harassed. Therefore, if an arrest or search contemplated under sections 41 and 42 is made under a warrant issued by any other Magistrate or is made by any officer not empowered or authorised, it would per se be illegal and would affect the prosecution case and consequently, vitiate the trial." 

 13. In the decision it has further been held, section 50 confers a valuable right on the person to be searched in the presence of a Gazetted Officer or a Magistrate if he so requires, since such a search would impart much more authenticity and creditworthiness to the proceedings while equally providing an important safeguard to the accused. To afford such an opportunity to the person searched, he must be aware of his right and that can be done only by the authorised officer informing him. Under the Act wide powers are conferred on the officers and deterrent sentence are also provided for the offences under the Act. The Legislature while keeping in view the menace of illicit drug trafficking deemed it fit to provide for corresponding safeguards to check the misuse of power thus conferred so that any harm to innocent persons is avoided and to minimise the allegations of planting or fabricating by the prosecution, section 50 is enacted. When such is the importance of a right given to an accused person in custody in general, the right by way of safeguard conferred under section 50 in the context is all the more important and valuable. Therefore, it is to be taken as an imperative requirement on the part of the officer intending to search. It must therefore, be held that on prior information the empowered officer or authorised officer while acting under section 41(2) or section 42 should comply with the provisions of section 50 before the search of the person is made and such per-son should be informed that if he so requires, he shall be produced before a Gezetted Officer or a Magistrate as provided thereunder. It is obligatory on the part of such officer to inform the person to be searched. Failure to inform the person to be searched and if such person so requires, failure to take him to the Gazetted Officer or the Magistrate, would amount to non-compliance of section 50 which is mandatory and thus it would affect the prosecution case and vitiate the trial. After being informed whether such person opted for such a course or not would be a question of fact. The provisions of section 50 are thus mandatory. 

 14. In the decision Nand Lal vs State of Rajasthan (1987) 3 Crimes 629, Raj) is a case where a police head constable and a station house officer were not empowered to carry out investigation and it was contended that the whole investigation was illegal and consequently the trial was vitiated. The Rajasthan High Court held that for launching the prosecution or for initiating the proceedings under the Act, the authority doing so must have a clear and unambiguous power. In Bhajan Singh vs State of Haryana (1988)1 Crimes 444 (PdH) it was observed that only officers empowered under the Act can take steps regarding entry, search, seizure and arrest and that the relevant provisions of the Act are mandatory. In Umrao vs State of Rajasthan (1988) 2 RLW 25, 1988 RLR 796) it was held that the search made by a police constable without jurisdiction and investigation made by an officer not empowered, vitiate the trial. In Shanti Lal vs State of Rajasthan (1989) 1 Crimes 276 (Raj) it was similarly held that search and arrest made by SHO who was not authorised under the Act, were illegal. 

 15. Therefore, if an arrest or search contemplated under sections 41 and 42 is made under a warrant issued by any other Magistrate or is made by any officer not empowered or authorised, it would per se be illegal and would affect the prosecution case and consequently, vitiate the trial. 

 17. In the case of Govend Lal Chaggan Lal Patel vs Agricultural Product Market Committee, (1975) 2 SCC 426=AIR 1976 SC 263 it was observed: 

 "Thus, the governing factor is the meaning and intent of the Legislature, which should be gathered not merely from the words used by the Legislature but from a variety of other circumstances and considerations. In other words, the use of the word 'shall' or 'may' is not conclusive on the question whether the particular requirement of law is mandatory or directory. But the circumstance that the Legislature has used a language of compulsive force is always of great relevance and in the absence of anything contrary in the context indicating that a permissive interpretation is permissible, the statute ought to be construed as peremptory. One of the fundamental rules of interpretation is that if the words of a statute are themselves precise and unambiguous, no more is necessary than to expound those words in their natural and ordinary sense, the words themselves in such case best declaring the intention of the Legislature. 

 18. The object of NDPS Act is to make stringent provisions for control and regulation of operations relating to those drugs and substances. At the same time, to avoid harm to the innocent persons and to avoid abuse of the provisions by the officers, certain safeguards are provided which in the context have to be observed strictly. Therefore, these provisions make it obligatory that such of those officers mentioned therein, on receiving an information, should reduce the same to writing and also record reasons for the belief while carrying out arrest or search as provided under the proviso to section 42(1). To that extent they are mandatory. Consequently, the failure to comply with these requirements thus affects the prosecution case and therefore, vitiates the trial." 

 20. Since the case has been investigated by an officer of RAB, who is not in any way sub-ordinate to the Director General of Narcotics Control Board, we are of the view that the entire proceeding from investigation and thereafter is vitiated. 

 22. The proceeding of Druta Bichar Tribunal Case No. 4 and 13 of 2008 pending in the court of Druta Bichar Tribunal No. 4, Dhaka are quashed. 

 The accused petitioner Amin Huda, son of Dr Zulfikar Huda, be set at liberty at once if the accused petitioner is not wanted in connection with any other case.
